newsitem.title: GERMANY: BZW says Telekom shares worth below 30 DM.
newsitem.headline: BZW says Telekom shares worth below 30 DM.

text.p: Stockbrokers BZW said on Friday that shares to be issued in the initial public offering of Deutsche Telekom AG were worth substantially less than the 30 marks-plus indicated by Telekom management.
In a report BZW Research said a valuation range based on a comparison with other European communications firms' earnings would put the shares at between 10.4 marks and 21.6 marks.

Telekom has debts of $67 billion -- the second highest for any company in the world and larger than the Turkish national debt -- meaning "it has many of the characteristics of a leveraged buy out", BZW said.

The heavy debt load will make the stock very sensitive to changes in regulation or capital spending. Taking those factors into account, BZW came up with a second model valuing the share at between 15.6 marks and 29.2 marks.

The IPO is planned for November and Telekom is authorised to sell up to one billion new shares, equivalent to 50 percent of existing capital. Existing shares can also be sold off as long as the state's holding does not fall below half.

BZW, which is not part of the global banking consortium formed to place the issue, said it expected around 500 million new shares to be issued in the first of two tranches. Forty percent of those are expected to go to small investors.
Telekom released figures in August showing that small investors could buy a maximum of 300 shares at a reduced rate for a combined price of 10,000 marks -- implying a sale price of 33 marks.
The report gave no investment recommendation, saying there were still too many unknown factors and stressing the valuations were based on theoretical models.

A BZW spokesman said in response to a Reuters inquiry that the real market price could be higher -- for example due to demand from investors looking to reflect the German stock market in their portfolios.

Telekom's debt mountain has piled up due to the largely political decision to upgrade eastern Germany's phone network to western standards following reunification at a cost of 50 billion marks ($33 billion).

Germany's telecoms market will be deregulated in 1998. BZW anticipates Telekom losing an annual three percent market share until 2005 and suffering price erosion of inflation less seven percent. Still, strong overall market growth will mean Telekom enjoys an annual turnover increase of 2.2 percent, BZW said.
Companies like engineering group Mannesmann AG, utilities RWE AG, VIAG and Veba AG and steel giant Thyssen AG are jockeying to enter the potentially lucrative German telecoms market.

But Deutsche Telekom has already taken a pre-emptive step to hold onto its market share by slashing 40 percent off charges for business customers. "Deutsche Telekom's strong cash generation and entrenched position in this very profitable industry makes it a formidable competitor," the report said.

One of Telekom's main strengths is its high revenues per phone line, and cost-cutting measures including annual job cuts of 10,000 workers for the next five years could help wipe out some outstanding debts.
BZW said a substantial charge is expected to be included in first half results due for publication on September 16 to cover early retirement costs.
It forecast that operating profits would fall to 14.9 billion marks this year from 18.4 billion last year, before recovering to a projected 19.2 billion in 1999.
